questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x$  that satisfies  $y(-3)=1.$  Assume that $y>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x \\ \int y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int y\text{d}y & =\int x\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+2{C}_{1} \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}+2{C}_{1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming $y>0,$ the general solution is

$$
y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+C},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(-3)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+C} \\ 1 & =\sqrt{9+C} \\ C & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x$ that satisfies the condition $y(-3)=1$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-8}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}$  that satisfies $y(1)=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2} \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{3} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where   $C=3{C}_{1}$ is an arbitrary constant.  

We now apply the condition $y(1)=2$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{3} & ={1}^{3}+C \\ 8-1 & =C \\ C & =7\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}={x}^{3}+7.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y$  that satisfies $y(0)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{x+C}\, \\ y & =\pm {e}^{x+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(0)=1$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =K{e}^{0} \\ K & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=y$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{x}\,.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =2\sqrt{x}+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{2\sqrt{x}+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{2\sqrt{x}+C}\, \\ |y| & ={e}^{2\sqrt{x}}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =K{e}^{2\sqrt{x}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the condition $y(1)={e}^{2}$ to find $K:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & =K{e}^{2\sqrt{1}} \\ {e}^{2} & =K{e}^{2} \\ K & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{x}}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)={e}^{2}$ is

$$
y={e}^{2\sqrt{x}}\,.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-{y}^{2} \\ -\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{y} & =x+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{x+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x+C},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{1+C} \\ 1+C & =1 \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{2}=0$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{y}^{3}=4x$ that satisfies $y(0)=1.$  Assume that $y>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{y}^{3} & =4x \\ 3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x(2+{y}^{3}) \\ \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=2+{y}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{2+{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2} & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3}) & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}} \\ 2+{y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{3} & =K{e}^{{0}^{2}}-2 \\ 1 & =K-2 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}=3{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x}{e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{-x} \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =-{e}^{-x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{-x}+C).\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the condition $y(0)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(-{e}^{0}+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(C-1) & =0 \\ C-1 & =1 \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{-x-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=0$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-{e}^{-x}).
$$

questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x}=3$ that satisfies $y(0)=-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3+2x{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{e}^{-x}+2x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{e}^{-x}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \,\text{d}y & =\int 3{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x+\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ y & =-3{e}^{-x}+{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=-3$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =-3 \\ -3{e}^{-0}+{0}^{2}+C & =-3 \\ C-3 & =-3 \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of ${e}^{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{e}^{x}=3$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=-3$ is

$$
y={x}^{2}-3{e}^{-x}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\frac{1}{xy}+\frac{2}{y})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 \\ \frac{2x-1}{xy}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x}{2x-1} \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2+\frac{2}{2x-1} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =(2+\frac{2}{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (2+\frac{2}{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ y & =K(2x-1){e}^{2x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)={e}^{2}$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & ={e}^{2} \\ K(2(1)-1){e}^{2(1)} & ={e}^{2} \\ K{e}^{2} & ={e}^{2} \\ K & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=(2x-1){e}^{2x}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{-y} & =6{x}^{2}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}-{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(6{x}^{2}-1){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =(6{x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (6{x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & =2{x}^{3}-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}-x+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}-x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=0$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot {1}^{3}-1+C) & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1+C) & =0 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{3}-x).
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $y' = 5y$ that satisfies $y(0)=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5y \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5 \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =5\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =5x+C\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm {e}^{5x+C} \\  & =\pm {e}^{C}{e}^{5x} \\  & =K{e}^{5x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm e^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

Now we apply the condition $y(0) = 3$ to find $K\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3 \\ K{e}^{5\cdot 0} & =3 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $y' = 5y$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=3$ is

$$
y = 3 e^{5x}  \,.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\cos(3y)\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \sin(2x) = 0$ given that  $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0.$ Assume that $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} < y < \dfrac{\pi}{6} .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution, and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3y)\,\text{d}y & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+C \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3y) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1=3C.$

Now let's apply the condition $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0$ to find $C_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot 0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0) & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{C}_{1} \\ 0 & =0+{C}_{1} \\ {C}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
\sin(3y)   =  \dfrac {3} {2} \cos(2x)
$$
